I know, it's a bit complicate. For what I was talking about, there are bound and unbound delegates. Each state has rules about this. Some are all bound, all unbound, and some are split. Pennsylvania, for example, has a few that are bound and then a bunch that are unbound.

When at the convention, the delegates vote and the person who reaches 1237 gets the nomination. The bound delegates have to vote for the winner of their district. The unbound ones can vote for whoever they want. It's basically bribery (ex: I'll give you one ride on air force one if you vote for me at the convention) for the unbound delegates. Some have integrity and vote for the winner of their district regardless of what they are bribed with. However, it's just a promise. Nothing is locked in so they can change their mind whenever. The only delegate votes that can be counted on are the bound delegates.

To make it more complicated, if no one reached 1237 after the first vote at the convention, they all (maybe it's most) become unbound. Sometimes the delegates are bound for X amount of voting rounds, but that is a state by state rule. So it becomes a mad rush to bribe people. When people talk about Cruz's shenanigans, they are referring to him getting promises from the delegates for the second round of voting and getting the unbound delegates to vote for him on the first round. Delegates usually advertise who they support so voters can be sure to vote for them but they can lie about it so I don't take it seriously.

Overall, it is best to have 1237 bound delegates on the first ballot to ensure nothing crazy can happen. Layers upon layers of rules. It's unfortunate that it can't be more straight forward. With how public this has all been on both sides of the isle, I would hope that a simplified system will be implemented in the future.
